extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, scientific method, and empirical inquiry (philosophy/science readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing and avoiding errors in observation, induction, and inference when conducting or evaluating empirical reasoning; covers a priori fallacies, non-observation, mal-observation, and principles for sound generalization. Useful for anyone learning scientific method or critical thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a priori fallacies (do not infer resemblance between cause and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the presumption that properties of an effect must be true of its cause (or vice versa). The maxim 'Tout ce qui est vrai de l’effet, est vrai de la cause' is given as an example of this mistaken principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives many historical examples (Victor Cousin, Coleridge, Spinoza, Leibnitz, Malebranche, Descartes, Cicero) showing how assuming homogeneity between cause and effect produces error (e.g., inferring that mind and matter cannot interact because they share no common property, or deducing physical order from supposed qualities of the Godhead). Beware of using theological or a priori notions of perfection to reject empirical facts (e.g., 'God is perfect, therefore nature must be perfect').

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate phenomena with their supposed physical correlates (distinguish effect from cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid defining a mental phenomenon as identical to the physical state thought to produce it (e.g., saying ideas 'are' animal motions of the organs of sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful whether you are speaking of the conscious effect (idea) or the supposed physical cause (state of nerves/brain). Confusing the two leads to category errors and obscures whether an account is about experience or about physiological mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against non‑observation of instances (overlooking counterinstances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-observation occurs when relevant instances that would affect the conclusion are overlooked—either entire instances or classes of instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes neglecting negative cases that falsify a claim (e.g., ignoring instances where a fortune-teller's predictions failed). The passage stresses the need for Elimination of Chance: remembering only confirming coincidences can sustain false beliefs (examples: almanac predictions, quack-doctors). Always seek the full set of instances before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against non‑observation of circumstances (overlooking important conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-observation can be of material circumstances in observed instances—facts that, if noticed, would change the interpretation of the instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: failing to note collusion in fulfilled predictions; phlogiston theory failed because gaseous combustion products were not observed; the 'sympathetic powder' cures were really due to wound dressing and rest; John Wesley attributing recovery to remedies while ignoring rest. Always look for concurrent causes, hidden conditions, and alternative explanations before attributing an effect to a claimed cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconceived opinions bias observation
rubrics_metrics.description: A preconceived theory or belief causes observers to attend only to facts that confirm it and to ignore contradictory facts, often even those plainly observable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include travelers who 'see' only what they expected in a foreign country, readers who miss contradictions in sacred texts, partisan historians, and cultural superstitions (e.g., coral changing color with health). Be aware that theory-laden perception will filter what is noticed; actively attempt to seek disconfirming evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value negative instances when forming axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative instances (cases that show a proposed universal to be false) have special force in establishing or refuting axioms and should not be neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes a human bias to be more moved by affirmative than negative instances, but for constructing true axioms the 'major vis' lies with negative instances. Explicitly search for and weigh counterexamples when building general claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mal‑observation — do not mistake inference for perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Mal-observation occurs when something seen is interpreted wrongly because inference is mistaken for direct perception; i.e., the observer reports inferences as if they were sense-data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic example: opponents of Copernicus 'saw' the sun rise and set and treated that appearance as proof, failing to recognize those are appearances compatible with multiple theories. Witnesses commonly mix inference with perception. In reports and testimony, separate what was directly perceived from what is inferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train to discriminate sensation from inference in observations and reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate observation requires practice and analytic habits to identify raw sensations apart from the interpretations built upon them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability is cultivated by disciplines (e.g., painters trained to note visual sensations; physicians trained to give 'specification unsophisticated by fancy'). Novices (and many practitioners) tend to couch observations in theoretical language; strive for clear, minimal descriptions of phenomena and label where inference begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider indirect, diffused, or secondary consequences (do not focus only on immediate obvious effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging social, economic, or institutional effects, include secondary and widely diffused consequences that may be opposite in sign to the immediate visible effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: apparent employment from lavish spending (A) vs. the employment sustained by investment/savings (B); the free-trade example where purchase of foreign goods induces export of equivalent value and thereby home employment. Observers often see only direct, localized effects and hence draw the wrong policy conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure generalizations conform to correct inductive principles (avoid principle-level misconceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors of generalization that are properly 'fallacies' arise from fundamental misconceptions about how induction works; casual lapses are blunders, but fallacies reflect mistaken conceptions of inductive method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before generalizing, confirm that the inductive conditions (adequate evidence, decisive instances, proper elimination of alternatives, attention to relevant circumstances) can in principle be met. Some kinds of generalization cannot be established by experience because the necessary conditions cannot be provided; recognize these limits.
